default.p.n1-dokkai-10-1.vietnamese:
More than 20 years ago, a Korean exchange student told me that Japan was lagging behind in cashless payments. He had planned to use a credit card when discharged from a prestigious university hospital in Japan, but his card was refused. He was reportedly stunned that something taken for granted in South Korea was impossible in a country considered developed like Japan. Even today, Japan remains stuck in its old ways: the cashless payment rate is only about 25%. The government plans to raise it to 40% toward Expo 2025 Osaka-Kansai and gradually increase it to 80% afterward. Cashless payments developed rapidly in South Korea because government policies gave consumers incentives to pay by card. Even so, I cannot help admiring how this method has spread in China to even the smallest shops. In Japan today, some people say they do not want to visit places that do not accept cards because it is inconvenient, while others do not want to touch cash because of COVID-19. The growing number of online shoppers will probably also contribute to the shift toward cashless payments. Since cash on delivery incurs an additional service fee, most people use cards as a matter of course, except those who are extremely concerned about Internet security.

As for me, I use a card when shopping online, while at physical stores I switch between cards and cash depending on the shop. Some stores issue their own credit cards, which give a 3% discount when payment is deducted from a bank account. Transportation cards, which save the trouble of buying train and bus tickets, are also convenient. I always carry these two cards. However, it is not that I never use cash; I may actually use it more often. Super-discount stores are already inexpensive, and they offer an additional 3% discount for cash payments. Prepared foods in particular are very cheap. For example, the French cheese I regularly eat every day usually costs 318 yen and sometimes only 299 yen, while it costs 438 or 468 yen at other shops, and even 398 yen at the supermarket mentioned above. There are many cash-oriented discount stores like these throughout Japan, so cash payments seem unlikely to disappear.

The shift to cashless payments benefits both customers and stores. For customers, the most important benefit is safety because they do not have to carry large amounts of money. For stores, it can shorten work such as closing shifts and reconciling the cash register, as well as prevent embezzlement and theft of sales revenue. Moreover, in a survey of foreign tourists, about 70% said they would have spent more if cashless payment had been available, so the benefits are even greater at tourist destinations. On the negative side, customers may overspend or have their cards used fraudulently. For stores, the high fees paid to card companies are a serious problem, but amid the current labor shortage, preparing change, counting cash, and giving change also represent significant costs. Should these advantages and disadvantages not be weighed against each other? For the country, cashless payments are beneficial because they can reduce the cost of printing and minting money and decrease the circulation of counterfeit currency. The greatest benefit may be a reduction in tax evasion.

There may be many ways to promote cashless payments, but even if the aim is different, as in India, I do not want crude measures such as abolishing high-denomination banknotes. When implementing such a policy, I think offering incentives—the “giving candy” approach used in South Korea—would be effective, but the method must be adjusted to suit Japan.

default.p.n1-dokkai-11-1.vietnamese:
A

As Japan enters a super-aged society, situations requiring death with dignity are becoming increasingly common. Everyone wishes to avoid a situation in which they have no hope of recovery but continue merely to breathe faintly. Discussions have also been held in the National Diet, and a "Bill Respecting Patients' Wishes Regarding End-of-Life Medical Treatment" was drafted. It clearly defined life-sustaining measures and "not initiating life-sustaining measures" for patients nearing death. It applied to people aged 15 and over, while people with intellectual disabilities and mental disorders were excluded. It also included a provision exempting doctors from liability when they did not initiate or discontinued life-sustaining measures. Death with dignity is intended to respect the patient's own wishes and help them face death with dignity, but because of sensitive issues such as reducing medical costs and elderly care, as well as numerous objections, the matter had to be handled cautiously and the bill was postponed. In actual medical practice, however, although peaceful death is not officially recognized, it is said that many doctors will still agree if there is a "Declaration of Intent Regarding Death with Dignity." Therefore, I think people who do not want to undergo excessive life-sustaining measures should make preparations in advance.

B

In Japan, death with dignity has not yet been legalized. However, as the number of people wishing for death with dignity increases year by year, more than 80% of the population now wants it to be legalized. In the medical community, the view that death with dignity should be permitted if the patient, family, and doctor all agree is also gradually spreading. Therefore, while they are still able to express their wishes, people who want life-sustaining measures to be limited or stopped at the end of life should prepare a "Declaration of Intent Regarding Death with Dignity" in advance. Since it has no legal force, nothing can be guaranteed with 100% certainty, but it is said that as many as 95% of doctors would currently agree. It is good for individuals to wish for death with dignity and prepare such a declaration, but legalizing it carries many potential problems. This is because people with severely impaired functions may have difficulty receiving sufficient support from those around them and may be forced to give up life-prolonging treatment because of a lack of support or pressure from others. If the law were passed, there would be a risk that people living with ventilators or feeding tubes would be driven into a situation in which they were forced to choose death with dignity. The invisible pressure weighing on them would be unavoidable. I hope for a society in which anyone can live, or die, in their own way.

default.p.n1-dokkai-12-1.vietnamese:
It is said that 26 of the world’s ultra-wealthy people possess assets equivalent to the combined wealth of approximately 3.8 billion low-income people worldwide. As a result, many people lament their poverty and feel unable to see a future. Poverty has spread even further around the world, especially since the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. To address this issue, the Pope in Rome and other influential figures around the world have proposed a “Basic Income” policy. Basic income means that the government guarantees a minimum standard of living for all citizens. It is a uniform, unconditional payment made regardless of age, gender, and so on. Every country probably has assistance programs for specific groups. Japan has many forms of public assistance, such as child-rearing support and welfare benefits for the poor, but it had never provided unconditional support to all citizens regardless of income until the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. When the special fixed benefit of 100,000 yen per person was paid, some questioned whether the wealthy should receive it too. However, imposing an income ceiling would make administrative procedures complicated, incur considerable costs, and delay the money reaching citizens. The government therefore decided to pay everyone on the grounds that those who did not need it could voluntarily decline it or donate it. The payments were also expected to circulate money and have a positive effect on the economy.

Basic income would both combat poverty and help address the declining birth rate. Because the payment would be made to everyone, the more children a family had, the more money it would receive. Although there are doubts about how effective this policy would be in raising the birth rate, given that the difficulties of raising children cannot be solved by money alone, the number would certainly increase compared with today. Furthermore, if people’s livelihoods were guaranteed and they did not have to work in poor labor conditions, working conditions would improve, and everyone could work in a way suited to them. In other words, people would be free to choose from a wider range of lifestyles.

The first disadvantage is the need for a huge budget. In Japan, a payment of 70,000 yen per person has been proposed, but it would require as much as 107 trillion yen a year. In addition, although this amount could be a windfall for people receiving small pensions, 70,000 yen would be a drastic reduction for those currently receiving welfare benefits, who receive an average of 140,000 yen per person, leaving them unable to make ends meet. Ultimately, the current welfare system would still have to remain. Since people could live without working, their motivation to work might decline, and the number of people unwilling to work could increase. It is obvious that taxes cannot be collected from people who do not work. Moreover, because Japan currently depends on foreign workers due to labor shortages, this would create enormous difficulties. To secure workers, wages would have to be raised, reducing corporate profits and competitiveness. The government would also have to raise taxes to secure revenue, forcing businesses to pass the higher taxes on to the prices of goods and services and making them increasingly less competitive. This would ultimately lead to rising prices.

Introducing basic income in financially strained Japan is impossible. It would be ideal to expand public assistance considerably so that everyone with below-average income could receive support, but that too can be said to be impossible. Moreover, if the policy were actually introduced, I feel that unforeseen problems, such as divisions among the public, would arise.

default.p.n1-dokkai-9-1.vietnamese:
The first Asian song to become a worldwide bestseller was Sakamoto Kyu's song 「SUKIYAKI」, which reached number one on the U.S. Billboard chart in 1963. In fact, before it reached the United States, the song had been released in Europe under its original Japanese title, 「Ue o muite arukou」, and had failed. The reason was that people did not understand what the title meant. Therefore, in the United States, the song was renamed 「SUKIYAKI」. Perhaps because Americans were familiar with the dish sukiyaki, the song was more readily accepted. This was a strategic success.

Today, although the circumstances are completely different from those of that time, a "global strategy" is still essential. K-pop, represented by BTS, is sweeping across the world market, and behind it lies a carefully calculated strategy. For example, BTS attracted Americans with lively music combining hip-hop and EDM, which are popular worldwide, along with powerful choreography. Although their songs were still mainly in Korean, their popularity grew even further when they released the English song 「Dynamite」 in 2020 with a message about overcoming difficult times together.

Their clothing and props also evoke nostalgia among Americans, making them easier to accept. Most important of all, however, is their extremely high quality. Their so-called "dagger choreography" is performed wonderfully, with the angles of their fingers and bodies and their timing synchronized like sword strokes, and their singing is also excellent. As a result, they quickly gained passionate popularity in the United States. YouTube has also played a major role as part of their strategy. Through YouTube, audiences around the world can access BTS and watch their performances from anywhere. Therefore, there is no reason not to use this tool. Then, after becoming fans, many people spread their excitement throughout the world via social media, creating an even stronger wave. This trend cannot be stopped. Looking back, what about Japan? I am worried that, unlike South Korea, Japan is becoming passive and neglectful simply because its domestic market is just large enough to sustain it.

（Note）うねり: The rolling of large waves.

Single-crystal ice, however, consists of one large crystal that has grown by freezing only from the top downward, forcing air bubbles and impurities toward the bottom. Impurities are said to accumulate easily in the gaps between crystals, but single-crystal ice has very few such spaces, so it contains no air bubbles and no impurities dissolve into the drink, making it completely transparent. That is why it is called the finest-tasting ice. Because it adds little unwanted flavor, it does not detract from the taste of whisky, for example. Bartenders who are particular about flavor therefore praise this ice highly. In addition, it melts very slowly, so drinks do not become diluted and lose their flavor right away. The drink’s original flavor is preserved for a long time. First, it should be marketed to bars, clubs, and high-end restaurants that place the greatest priority on the taste of their drinks. Once individuals understand the value of this ice, they will buy it too. I think the future of single-crystal ice is very bright.

In fact, this ice was created by a company in a completely unrelated industry. I would also like to add here—although I know it is somewhat extraneous—that the experience of a metal-accessories manufacturer was applied to making the metal plate for the special equipment essential to producing this ice.

（Note 1）Kachiwari-gōri: Ice made by breaking up a large block of ice used for drinking water...
（Note 2）Zatsumi: An impure taste that detracts from the original flavor of liquor, tea, coffee, and so on (such as excessive sourness, astringency, or bitterness).

default.p.n1-dokkai-9-3.vietnamese:
Everyone does this, but athletes in particular are always looking for the best clothing, shoes, and other equipment to use. Manufacturers also regard this as an important part of their business, because if an athlete achieves good results with a company’s product, it is not only a source of great joy; having the product used by athletes also raises the company’s profile and increases sales.

For example, many people probably still clearly remember how athletes wearing the 「LZR Racer」 swimsuit, which was highly water-repellent and tightly fitted to the body, repeatedly broke world records at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. World records were reset in 21 of the 32 events. The polyurethane coating on the surface smoothed out the body’s contours and significantly improved the athletes’ performance. The difference between athletes wearing this suit and those who were not was too obvious. This became an issue from the standpoint of fairness, and in 2010, the 「International Swimming Federation」 limited the parts of the body that could be covered and banned materials other than fabric. Even so, the competition to develop swimsuits that are lighter and tighten the abdomen to maintain a horizontal position continues today.

As for running shoes, in 2020, 「thick-soled shoes」 with a highly resilient composite-fiber plate in the sole became a controversial topic. When the performance of athletes wearing these shoes improved dramatically, World Athletics introduced regulations limiting the sole thickness for marathon races to no more than 40 mm and allowing a maximum of one plate. Although everyone may think that choosing one’s shoes is a matter of personal freedom, World Athletics rules require competition shoes to be reasonably accessible to all runners and prohibit them from providing unfair assistance or advantage.

In every field, products evolve day by day. Therefore, when a new product complies with the rules but makes it absolutely impossible for other competitors to win, the rules are changed again. In other words, this is an endless cycle of chasing one another.

(Note) Water repellency (撥水性): The ability to repel or prevent water from penetrating.

default.p.n2-dokkai-10-4.vietnamese:
Even with the same body shape, the type of clothing you wear can make you look heavier or slimmer. Warm colors make you look larger, while cool colors make you look smaller. There are ways of coordinating clothes that make you look slimmer. It is effective to wear clothes with a clear contrast in color, such as a white shirt paired with black pants. It is also effective to create vertical divisions with long vertical items of clothing. For example, if you wear a one-piece dress and put on a long coat over it with the front buttons left open, you will appear to have three slim, elongated vertical sections, making this highly effective. Therefore, vertically striped clothing is also very effective. In addition, a V-neck makes you look slimmer. These are all visual illusions, but we should make clever use of them.

(Note 1) Warm colors: Colors that look warm, such as red and orange
(Note 2) Cool colors: Colors that look cool, such as blue and light blue
(Note 3) Kiyase: Wearing clothes that make you look slimmer than you actually are

default.p.n2-dokkai-11-1.vietnamese:
Vitamin D is necessary for strengthening bones and maintaining muscles. It is also believed to be associated with the onset of influenza and cancer. The daily amount that needs to be obtained through food is approximately 5.5 μg. Vitamin D is found in mushrooms, seafood, eggs, and dairy products, but the highest amounts are found in fish. In the case of salmon, which is easy to buy year-round, eating one slice every two days is reportedly enough to provide about 30 μg. Some people may think that supplements are an effective way to increase their intake. However, because vitamin D is fat-soluble, taking too much can cause health problems. Hypercalcemia can occur, causing large amounts of calcium to accumulate in the blood vessels, kidneys, heart, lungs, and other parts of the body, which may lead to various symptoms. It is therefore important to be extremely careful. For this reason, obtaining vitamin D through daily meals is recommended. An even better option is exposure to ultraviolet rays—sunbathing—because vitamin D can be synthesized through the skin. If an area of skin roughly the size of the face and the backs of both hands is exposed to sunlight, the time required to synthesize 5.5 μg in Tokyo during summer, when ultraviolet radiation is strongest, around noon, is reportedly 3.5 minutes. In winter, it is about 22 minutes. Since Japan stretches from north to south, the corresponding times in Hokkaido are 4.6 minutes and 76 minutes, while in Okinawa they are 2.9 minutes and 7.5 minutes. People who completely cover themselves because they believe ultraviolet rays are harmful have no choice but to obtain vitamin D through food. However, those who want to avoid sunburn for cosmetic reasons need only expose parts of the body other than the face to sunlight.

（Note 1）μg: One-millionth of a gram (1/1,000,000 g)
（Note 2）One slice: A piece cut from something. For salmon, approximately 80〜150g
（Note 3）Dietary supplement: Something that supplies nutrients the body lacks, such as vitamin or calcium supplements
（Note 4）Fat-soluble vitamin: A vitamin that is difficult to dissolve in water and dissolves easily in oil
（Note 5）Hypercalcemia: A condition in which there is an abnormally high amount of calcium in the blood
（Note 6）Kidneys: Organs that remove unnecessary substances from the blood to produce urine
（Note 7）The backs of both hands: The outer sides of both hands, where the fingernails are; the sides opposite the palms
（Note 8）Protection: Here, preventing ultraviolet rays from reaching the body in order to protect it

default.p.n2-dokkai-11-2.vietnamese:
In the Kansai region, people sometimes add 「chan」 or 「san」 to the names of foods. The first time I heard 「Ame-chan」 (candy), I thought it sounded childish, but now I gradually find it rather endearing. People also add 「o」 or 「san」 to other foods, such as Oimo-san (sweet potatoes), Omame-san (beans), and Okayu-san (rice porridge), giving these names a gentler, warmer feeling. This practice seems to have originated with expressions once used by female attendants in the Kyoto Imperial Court, who spoke of food with appreciation, and later spread among ordinary people. Today, it is especially common for round and cute-looking foods. Rice porridge apparently falls into this category because the container it is served in is round. In addition, the fact that 「O~san」 is rarely used for foods with long names may be because they are difficult to pronounce.

「San」 is also attached to greetings such as 「Ohayou-san」 and 「Omedeto-san」. It is said that people use these expressions to show respect or concern for the other person. Moreover, people also call deities, the Buddha, the moon, and the sun 「Tenjin-san」, 「Kannon-san」, 「Ohisa-san」, and 「Otsuki-san」. In the Kanto region, these figures might instead be called 「Tenjin-sama」, for example. Kanto speakers use 「sama」, which can express stronger respect than 「san」. However, this does not mean that people in Kansai lack respect. I think they feel both respect and a sense of closeness and affection. In Kanto, people may feel that the other party is so noble that they cannot approach them. People also say 「Ouma-san」 (horse), but not 「Oushi-san」 (bull). This may be related to their feelings toward the owner. Perhaps 「O~san」 expresses both appreciation and close affection.

(Note 1) Female attendant in the imperial court: a female attendant serving in the imperial palace

(Note 2) Concern and care: paying close attention to someone and worrying about them

(Note 3) Deities and the Buddha: gods and the Buddha

The period during which an athlete can compete as an athlete is very short. After retirement, very few people can obtain jobs such as head coach, assistant coach, or commentator. These are coveted positions. If someone earns a great deal of money while still an athlete, they may be able to build rental apartments and live without financial difficulty. However, some athletes are forced to retire suddenly because of injury. Athletes employed by companies may be able to continue working there, but professional athletes may face difficulties in making a living afterward. They may also take a job at an ordinary company, but what they must be aware of then is that they will have to set aside their pride. No matter how brilliantly they shone in the world of sports, that achievement is not necessarily useful in other environments. So what should athletes prepare while they are still competing? Should they study foreign languages, bookkeeping, or various certifications generally considered necessary in society? Except in cases where someone lives abroad for a long time and naturally acquires foreign-language ability, they should first focus on what they are devoting themselves to now. That means studying their sport, seeking ways to improve their training, and solving everyday problems effectively in order to achieve their goals. This can also extend their athletic careers, making it a case of killing two birds with one stone. In the process, their ability to think and their mental resilience will be forged. This is the ability most necessary for life afterward—that is what I, someone who has watched many athletes, want to tell you.

（Note 1）Bookkeeping: recording a company's daily transactions and inflows and outflows of money, etc.
（Note 2）Forging/training: here, strict training to make one's skills, mind, and physical strength firm and resilient.

default.p.n2-dokkai-12-1.vietnamese:
A

Women's universities are extremely rare overseas. Even in the United States, which has more than 3,000 universities, the number of women's universities has fallen from around 200 to fewer than 40. In South Korea, there are only seven women's universities. Japan has followed the same trend. After reaching a peak of 98 universities in 1998, the number has fallen to 76 because of the declining birth rate and the growing preference among students for coeducational universities, where men and women study together. Nevertheless, women's universities still account for as much as 10% of all universities. In Japan, women's universities continue to have their own significance. Compared with coeducational universities, their greatest appeal is that smaller class sizes allow students to receive attentive support not only in their studies but also in finding employment. As a result, their employment rate is higher than that of coeducational universities. In addition, being able to accumulate experiences different from those available at coeducational universities over four years is also highly beneficial. At a coeducational university, leadership roles rarely go to female students, but at a women's university, students gain leadership experience, which proves very useful when they enter society. I believe this is precisely why, although fewer women graduate from women's universities than from coeducational universities, a remarkable number of women shine as leaders in society. Because there are no men watching them, students do not need to worry about their clothes or appearance and can feel very comfortable. Being able to concentrate seriously on their studies is another advantage.

B

I think both coeducational and single-sex universities have their own strengths, but coeducational universities have become more popular in recent years. Therefore, it is understandable that even prestigious women's universities, which were once very difficult to get into, have lost some of their standing. Nevertheless, I believe that studying at a women's university still offers major benefits that coeducational universities do not. In fact, I even feel that not having the opportunity to attend a women's university is a significant disadvantage. Even aside from their excellent employment rates, spending four important years in a society without gender discrimination—years that influence the formation of one's character and way of thinking—is a rare and valuable experience that will greatly affect one's way of life in the future. At a women's university, unlike at a coeducational university, women alone must work together to plan and carry out everything. Because both the planning and execution are handled entirely by women, students can experience countless different roles, beginning with taking the initiative to assume leadership. The opportunity to further develop one's abilities is one of the strengths of a women's university. People often say that there are few opportunities to socialize or date men, but I believe women's universities have advantages that far outweigh this point. In practice, interaction with students from other universities is very lively, so this concern is not really significant.

(Note) さほど: to that extent

default.p.n2-dokkai-13-1.outline.0.note: Introduces the scale and definition of small and medium-sized enterprises, explaining that most work as subcontractors for large corporations, exposing them to price pressure, lost orders, and bankruptcy. Question 69 is based here.

default.p.n2-dokkai-13-1.outline.2.label: A solution for survival: innovation through an outside perspective

default.p.n2-dokkai-13-1.outline.3.label: Vocabulary notes in the passage
default.p.n2-dokkai-13-1.outline.3.note: Explains technical terms and keywords from the passage: 下請け (subcontractor), シェア (market share), ゆるまない (not loosen), ネジ (screw), and 消費者のクレーム (consumer complaints).
default.p.n2-dokkai-13-1.vietnamese:
Small and medium-sized enterprises account for 99.7% of all businesses in Japan, and as many as 68.8% of the country’s workers are employed by them. In manufacturing, small and medium-sized enterprises are businesses with capital of 300 million yen or less or 300 employees or fewer; in the service industry, they have capital of 50 million yen or less or 100 employees or fewer. Businesses with even fewer employees—20 or fewer—are called small-scale enterprises. Although many Japanese small and medium-sized enterprises possess advanced technology, they work as subcontractors for large corporations. As a result, many lose orders to cheaper foreign companies, or are pressured by large corporations to lower their prices during economic downturns, making business difficult and sometimes leading to bankruptcy. Nevertheless, some small and medium-sized enterprises are exceptionally successful. Many hold the number-one market share and receive orders from around the world because they possess highly advanced technology that others cannot imitate. Others shine because they use their advanced technology to launch new products. For example, when one company successfully developed a “screw that never loosens,” it had only about 50 employees. The company that manufactured an ultra-small gear weighing one-millionth of a gram and astonished the world had only about 70 employees, while the company that produced painless injection needles, for which countless patients were grateful, had only six employees. All of these were truly very small companies.

Therefore, I believe that small and medium-sized enterprises should follow this path if they are to survive. For a company to proactively discover something unique to itself, it is essential to view things from an outside perspective. I believe opportunities will remain limited if companies continue as before, developing excellent products only when a talented person or a good idea happens to emerge internally. Holding meetings within the company is one good idea. Another possibility, I think, is to examine the consumer complaints flooding society. However, what can be done solely within a company is always limited. I believe it is important to ask outsiders to reassess the company’s technology. Naturally, consulting experts would be useful, but I feel that inviting opinions from ordinary people as well could lead to more interesting, truly unique products. Since this is the age of the internet, isn’t that possibility quite high?

(Note 1) Subcontracting (下請け): Accepting all or part of work that another person or company has undertaken; or the person or company performing such work.
(Note 2) Market share (シェア): Here, the percentage of the market represented by a company’s sales.
(Note 3) Does not loosen (ゆるまない): A state of fitting tightly without any gap.
(Note 4) Screw (ネジ): An object with a spiral groove around the outside of a cylindrical shaft, or an object with an inner groove designed to fit it. When the two fit together tightly, they do not shift.
(Note 5) Consumer complaints (消費者のクレーム): Here, customers’ statements that a product is unsatisfactory, such as saying that something is difficult to use or easily breaks.

In Sakura City, except for apartment complexes where garbage is managed by staff, garbage collection has been changed to door-to-door collection. The reason is that complaints have continually been sent to city hall about such problems as people not following the designated days and times for putting out garbage, failing to sort it beforehand, and leaving garbage scattered around. In addition, no one wants a garbage collection point located near their own home. Of course, most collection points were places where residents cleaned up together and had no complaints, but the rules were changed so that garbage would be left in places such as residents’ own yards. Garbage collectors now have to visit each household. Some people are also pleased with door-to-door collection for another reason: they are elderly people who used to have great difficulty traveling all the way to distant garbage collection sites.

(Note) 戸別収集: Collecting garbage by visiting each household.

default.p.n3-dokkai-5-1.vietnamese: A foreign friend once asked me why Japanese people so often immediately say 「すみません」. 「すみません」 is a very convenient word, so I often use it without thinking. Because it is easy to pronounce, people sometimes say 「すいません」 instead of 「すみません」. People generally think and are taught that 「すみません」 is used when apologizing, but it is also used when calling someone, asking for something, and thanking someone. It may be used even more often in these latter situations. This is because, as adults, people often use polite expressions such as 「申し訳ありません／申し訳ございません」 when apologizing. In business, it is normal to use these expressions when apologizing. 「すみません」 is also commonly used in stores when asking a staff member to come over or when making a request. When receiving something or when someone does something for us, people often say 「すみません」 to express thanks instead of saying 「ありがとう」. Some people also say that they prefer hearing 「ありがとう／ありがとうございます」. It seems that the use of 「すみません」 when calling someone, making a request, or expressing thanks stems from a feeling of being sorry toward the other person.

default.p.n3-dokkai-5-2.vietnamese:
Purikura is an abbreviation of “Print Club.” It is a type of machine that uses a camera to photograph a person’s face and print the image as stickers. It was introduced to the market in 1995. For 300 yen, users could print 16 photo stickers measuring 1.5 cm in height and 2.5 cm in width. Purikura became popular mainly among high school girls, and increasing numbers of young women began putting the stickers in notebooks to look at, show one another, or exchange while enjoying themselves. Sales reached approximately 60 billion yen in 2002, but after smartphones became widespread and people could take photos themselves, sales fell to about one-third. This was because smartphones allowed people to take photos anywhere and at any time without spending money. Even so, many young women still use Purikura. This is because Purikura has continued to evolve. Rather than simply preserving one’s appearance as it is, it can produce glamorous, “moreru” photos. The word “moru” originally means to pile up or make something fuller, but in youth language it commonly refers to editing photos to make someone look more attractive than in reality. It does not matter if the resulting photo does not look like the actual person. On the contrary, they enjoy the transformation itself. For 400 yen, Purikura provides the fun of taking photos, editing them, and adding text to the final images. Users can also use their smartphones to record or photograph themselves throughout the process. Furthermore, it is said that satisfaction increases even more when they upload the photos to social networking services (SNS) and attract people’s attention.

(Note 1) Editing: Here, changing the original appearance. It can make the skin look lighter, the eyes look larger, and recently can even change the shape of the face or the length of the legs.
(Note 2) SNS: An abbreviation of Social Networking Service, an online member service where registered users can communicate and interact with one another.

default.p.n3-dokkai-6-1.vietnamese: There are many countries in the world where tap water cannot be drunk, but Japan's tap water is said to be inexpensive, safe, and delicious. Nevertheless, bottled mineral water began selling very well around 1990. This was because the false impression that 「tap water is bad and dangerous」 spread widely on its own. From around 2010, it sold even better than coffee and tea, with annual sales reaching 320 billion yen. Even a cheap 500-milliliter bottle of mineral water costs 100 yen. Tap water, depending on the area, probably costs less than 1 yen. So why do people buy water? Because once an impression has spread, it is very difficult to change. In fact, tap water is safe, and it tastes good. Naturally, the taste differs depending on the water source—whether the river is clean, how much groundwater is mixed in, and so on—so water in rural areas is often tastier. And as people say, Tokyo's tap water was indeed poor for a time. Today, however, even breweries, which are extremely particular about their water sources, use Tokyo tap water. More than 60 water authorities, including Tokyo's, bottle tap water and sell it for around 100 to 120 yen, and it sells so well that the business is profitable. The result of a taste test conducted by the Tokyo Metropolitan Bureau of Waterworks, in which about 30,000 people drank water for comparison, was as follows: 39.1% said the tap water tasted better, 41% said the mineral water tasted better, and 19.8% said both tasted good. Therefore, I think there is no problem if people buy water for another reason, but there is no need to buy it simply because it tastes better. Moreover, the tastiness of water is also related to its temperature. Even mineral water will not taste good if it becomes warm, while tap water becomes very tasty when chilled. People should know things like this as well.

Last night, my whole family discussed social media (SNS) and established some family rules.

The basic SNS rules learned at school are to use it for no more than two hours a day and to be allowed to use it until 10:00 p.m.

In addition to these rules, my family added rules of our own.
They are not using SNS during meals, not using it while studying, and not meeting in person anyone encountered through social media.

We also decided together on punishments for failing to follow these five rules.
Both of my parents work, and I also have a part-time job. I can pay money as a punishment, but my younger sister, who is in junior high school, cannot do that yet.
Therefore, whenever I break a rule, I must pay 3,000 yen, while my sister must clean the bathroom.

In addition, we agreed that SNS may not be used on the day after a rule is broken.
